clue.text: Where prices fall, endless obligation on unhesitating poet is not ordered

indicators.note: a thing with no end has lost its final letter, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a duty is an obligation; endless drops its last letter

indicators.note: putting words in order means arranging them afresh, so these letters are rearranged
the hesitation sound er is removed, as a speaker who no longer hesitates drops it

parts.note: Geoffrey Chaucer, author of The Canterbury Tales; minus the hesitation er
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a duty laid on some poet has been carried out in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the crossword hesitation, so an unhesitating Chaucer is CHAUC. DUT + CHAUC + TIONS gives DUTCH AUCTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: In a Dutch auction the auctioneer starts high and lowers the asking price until some bidder accepts.

clue.text: Downtrodden like Old Labour?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: led by Michael Foot, Labour leader 1980 to 1983

explanation.surface: Was the old Labour Party, with its working-class roots, the party of the oppressed?
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Foot led the Labour Party before its New Labour rebranding, so Old Labour was literally UNDER FOOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something underfoot lies beneath people's feet and gets trampled, which is the literal picture behind downtrodden.

clue.text: Wrong number for Frost?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
rime is hoar frost

explanation.surface: A question whether some number, perhaps a poem or a TV episode, was the wrong choice for Frost.
explanation.walkthrough: Frost looks like the poet Robert Frost or the broadcaster David Frost, but it is just frozen dew.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime is a wrong, an offence against the law; the noun sense of wrong, not the adjective.

clue.text: Silver starting to develop problems

indicators.note: only the start of the next word is wanted, so its final letter is cut off

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
to grow is to develop; only its start is kept

explanation.surface: A silver item, perhaps tarnishing, beginning to show faults.
explanation.walkthrough: AGGRO is British slang, short for aggravation.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for trouble, hassle or aggressive bother, so it stands for problems.

clue.text: Singer can use the letters

indicators.note: using the letters of a phrase means taking them as raw material to spell a new word

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer is allowed to make use of written letters, perhaps lyrics.
explanation.definitionFit: A chanteuse is a female singer, especially one performing popular songs in a nightclub or cabaret.

clue.text: Charges for a large quantity of fruit

parts.note: a, meaning one, is I in Roman numerals
M is a thousand in Roman numerals
peaches are a fruit

explanation.surface: What a greengrocer charges for a big load of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Charges looks like prices on a market stall; it is the verb, to accuse formally.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach someone is to accuse a public official formally of misconduct, so impeaches means charges.

clue.text: One complaint raised by Old Testament character

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising the letters reads them from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a moan is a complaint

explanation.surface: A biblical figure lodges a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Naomi complained in the Book of Ruth that the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her.
explanation.definitionFit: Naomi is Ruth's mother-in-law in the Book of Ruth, part of the Hebrew scriptures.

clue.text: Getting things just so, like Chopin after his love embraced mine

definitions.note: a phrase for the activity; the answer is a noun for fastidious smartness

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: George Sand, the novelist, was Chopin's lover
a pit is a coal mine
Chopin was born in Poland

explanation.surface: Chopin, a perfectionist, compared with his lover holding something of the speaker's.
explanation.walkthrough: Love looks like a pet name, but it means a lover; 'after' tells you the nationality comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Spit and polish is the scrupulous cleaning and smartness of a soldier's kit, making everything perfect.

clue.text: Disease and its cause, an ego like the French

parts.note: a germ causes disease
taken as written
the ego is the self, me
as means like
les is French for the (plural)

explanation.surface: A medical note on an illness and its origin, in self-centred French style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the definition to the run of pieces: GERM + AN + ME + AS + LES.
explanation.definitionFit: German measles is the common name for rubella, a mild viral infection producing a rash.

clue.text: Unnecessary verbiage for weightless bear

indicators.note: less means without, so a word for a unit of weight is taken away

parts.note: Paddington is the marmalade-loving bear of children's books; remove TON, a weight

explanation.surface: A wordy description of a bear who floats in zero gravity.
explanation.walkthrough: The ton is a unit of weight, so without it the bear leaves PADDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Padding is material added to writing or speech only to make it longer, adding length without substance.

clue.text: Pass — turn over a couple of pages first

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to turn something is to twist it into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: pp is the abbreviation for pages
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to a reader to skip ahead after first flipping two pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' puts A and PP ahead of the reworked word over.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass a bill or proposal is to approve it formally, as a parliament or committee does.

clue.text: Cast heard to be suffering

indicators.note: heard means the word counts only by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: to cast is to throw

explanation.surface: A theatre cast reported to be in distress.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast looks like a group of actors; it is the verb, to fling.
explanation.definitionFit: A throe is a violent spasm of pain, and in throes means in the midst of agony or struggle.

clue.text: Cutting mat with scissors — all but the ends, strangely

indicators.note: something done strangely is out of its usual order, so the letters are rearranged
everything except the extremes is kept, so the first and last letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then trimmed of its outer letters

explanation.surface: Trimming a mat with scissors in an odd way, leaving the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: Cutting looks like the act with scissors, but it is the social sense, as in cutting someone dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting someone means snubbing or ignoring them; ostracism is exclusion from society, the same deliberate cold shoulder.

clue.text: Return to the point before long — it may be catching

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: soon means before long
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An instruction to get back to the matter in hand quickly, with a warning about something contagious.
explanation.walkthrough: Catching looks like infectious, but it means trapping, as a snare does.
explanation.definitionFit: A noose is a loop with a running knot used to snare animals, so it is a device for capturing.

clue.text: Running away with strange men to Peel

indicators.note: strange suggests something altered from its normal form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Fleeing with odd men towards Peel, a town on the Isle of Man, or to Robert Peel's police.
explanation.definitionFit: An elopement is a secret flight from home to marry, a running off with a lover.

clue.text: Our ends may be (Hamlet) — when's possible clue?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a quotation from Hamlet about how we shape our ends ourselves
second meaning: read as a clue itself, rough says to jumble the following four letters into the word when

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says there's a divinity that shapes our ends, 'rough-hew them how we will'. Read as a clue, ROUGH HEWN is rough (anagram) + HEWN, giving WHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-hewn means shaped crudely, cut roughly into form, which is what Hamlet says we do to our ends.

clue.text: Oven to be held by judge: that's where it's done

definitions.note: loose: the dish that gets done in the oven held inside it

indicators.note: something held by another is gripped inside it, so these pieces go within

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a game
an oast is a kiln for drying hops
taken as written

explanation.surface: An oven is going to be inspected by a judge, who says that is where the work happens.
explanation.walkthrough: Oven is a kiln for hops here, not a kitchen oven; the definition is loose, the dish being what gets done.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef is a joint cooked in an oven, so it is the thing done, meaning cooked, there.

clue.text: Master Blair's retained hanging for those in 1, 8, 9 and 26

indicators.note: to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece keeps another inside it

parts.note: Euan Blair, Tony Blair's eldest son; Master is the title for a boy
the rope is a hangman's instrument
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's young son kept a wall hanging intended for certain people.
explanation.walkthrough: The entries at 1, 8, 9 and 26 begin DUTCH, POLISH, GERMAN and BRITISH, all nationalities of the continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch, Polish, German and British people all live on the same continent, so collectively they are its inhabitants.

clue.text: The regular custom of sponsorship?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the trade a shop gets from its regular customers
second meaning: the support given by a patron

explanation.walkthrough: Custom looks like a habit or tradition; here it means the business customers bring.
explanation.definitionFit: Patronage is both the support of a sponsor for an artist or cause and a business's steady clientele.

clue.text: A romp through Berlin?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a lively outing or binge
second meaning: the river that flows through the German capital

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a night out in Berlin; the question mark flags that the second meaning is something that literally runs through the city.
explanation.definitionFit: A spree is a bout of unrestrained fun, and the Spree is the river running through central Berlin.

clue.text: Theatrical musician and literary baron allowed back in

definitions.note: two separate senses: a theatre's name and a musician's surname

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: Edward Bulwer-Lytton, novelist, was made Baron Lytton

indicators.note: back means the word is read the wrong way, end to start

parts.note: let means allowed

explanation.surface: A list of people: a stage musician, and a writing nobleman readmitted.
explanation.walkthrough: LYT(TEL)TON. The Lyttelton is one of the National Theatre's stages in London; Humphrey Lyttelton was a jazz trumpeter and radio host.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a London theatre auditorium and to Humphrey Lyttelton, the British jazz trumpeter and bandleader.

clue.text: Present, maybe, making one uptight

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the present is one example of a verb form for time

explanation.surface: A gift that leaves the recipient nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: Present looks like a gift; it is the grammatical time of a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Present is a grammatical tense, alongside past and future, and tense also means anxious and nervy.

clue.text: The lowest point in deception, a dirty business

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the following run of words, spanning them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of deception, the word a and the start of dirty
surface padding, completing the phrase dirty business

explanation.surface: Deceit as a grubby trade reaching rock bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the bottom of a decline, originally the point of the sky directly underfoot.

clue.text: Student well informed on American disease

parts.note: L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
up in a subject means knowledgeable about it
US stands for the United States

explanation.surface: A well-read student studying an American illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lupus is an autoimmune illness that can cause inflammation of the skin, joints and organs.

clue.text: Not a load-bearing beam

definitions.meaning: first meaning: carrying no heavy burden, not weighty
second meaning: a ray of illumination

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a building term for a girder that carries no weight; beam is really a ray.
explanation.definitionFit: Light means weighing little, unburdened, and also a beam of light shining from a source like a torch.

clue.text: Genuine error by Wax?

parts.note: a sin is a moral error
cere is an old word for wax, as in cerecloth

explanation.surface: A real mistake made by a wax model, or by a man named Wax.
explanation.walkthrough: Sincere is popularly said to come from Latin sine cera, without wax, which makes 'error by wax' a nice twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sincere means honest and free of pretence, so genuine in feeling or manner.

clue.text: Lower with awful dread, for example

indicators.note: awful suggests something badly made, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
e.g. is the abbreviation for for example

explanation.surface: Bringing someone down with terrible fear, as an illustration.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade is to reduce in rank, quality or dignity, so it means to lower or debase.

clue.text: Sh! Tebbit is for reform? You'll be lucky!

indicators.note: to reform is to form again in a different shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the thirteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hushed retort to the idea that Norman Tebbit, a hard-line Conservative minister, favours reform.
explanation.walkthrough: Best of British, short for best of British luck, is said ironically to someone attempting the near-impossible.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a sardonic good-luck wish meaning you have no chance, the same sense as you'll be lucky.
